utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is hearing this part of the session in open session only to make this ruling: The circumstances having changed, we shall hear the rest of this witness's evidence in closed session, the Trial Chamber being satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to do so. We shall go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We have ruled on this matter. We ruled without argument. It's an extremely serious situation and one which we must take prompt action. Now, yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, yesterday we concluded, or you concluded your testimony speaking about leaving Zvornik -- I'm sorry, leaving Visegrad and speaking about an event that happened as you left Visegrad. Sometime after you left Visegrad, did you return to Zvornik and attempt to enter the town of Zvornik once again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was on the 10th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you during your testimony to describe a number of locations in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And to assist the Chamber, I'm going to ask that the witness be shown Exhibit 342, tab 4, and ask that it be placed on the overhead projector. And I'd ask if the director could zoom out so that we can see more of the map. That's good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, does this map indicate a rough representation of the streets of the city of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to point, for the Chamber, to the bridge crossing from Mali Zvornik into Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, prior to your testimony before the Chamber, were you asked to label this map with a number of markings to indicate different places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you indicate the bridge with the number C4-1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want you to next indicate to the Chamber the location of the headquarters of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us what number you used to indicate that location?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat that number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, could you please repeat that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you indicate the place where you will testify regarding a meeting you had with a person by the name of Cele?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not far from where it is indicated on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you marked that on the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you please indicate where the Ciglani brick factory is located.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how did you mark that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Ciglani brick factory is here. D4-4.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that D4 or C4 with which you marked that location?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the letter, please? We're not sure if it's D or T.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the letter that you used to indicate that location.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With a C.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I asked you to indicate the area of Celopek. Perhaps if the map can be moved over to the left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Celopek is on this road towards Zvornik, and it is marked with C4-5.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dulovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that that be left on the overhead, but I won't be asking any questions now or in the immediate future.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, when you returned to Zvornik area, can you describe what, if anything, was remarkable about the Mali Zvornik side of the Drina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the side of Mali Zvornik, on the bridge, towards the end of the bridge, on that side, there was a line-up of sacks of sand, sandbags, and there were people there, some of them in uniform, others not in uniform, in civilian clothing, and on top of these sandbags was a machine-gun and a soldier who had -- was targeting the opposite side, the Muslim side. He had his machine-gun pointing in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've described seeing uniformed people there. Can you identify -- or can you identify the units or institutions they were from by their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or, rather, some of it I could see and not the others. I could distinguish the police uniforms and the military uniforms. I was able to distinguish those. The man at the machine-gun was wearing a military uniform or, rather, a camouflage army uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the men in police uniforms, were they from the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the soldier told me, the one that I had a lengthy conversation with who was up by the machine-gun, manning that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the purpose of this particular visit to the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to see what was going on in Zvornik, because at that time, there was large-scale propaganda to the effect that the Serbian population in Zvornik was threatened and that crimes were being committed against them, and I wanted to see for myself whether that was true or not, because it didn't sound very convincing, what the papers were writing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at the bridge, can you tell us what, if anything, you noticed about the bridge was different this time you were at Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the other side of the bridge, there was a plaque or sign turned towards the Serb side, and on that plaque, it said "Republika Srpska." That was written up on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you attempt to cross the bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was no problem. They allowed me to go through and I passed across the bridge. Before that, they had advised me that I was going at my own risk and suggested that I should not cross the bridge to go into the Muslim side, cautioned me against it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Prior to crossing the bridge, did you have a conversation with the person behind the machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I talked to that soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us in substance what he told you about the situation at the bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me or, rather, I asked him why that machine-gun was pointing to the other side when it says "Republika Srpska" there, and he told me that they were on the bridge because there were various paramilitaries or other units who were trying by force to cross the bridge. They had tried several times with weapons and with what they had seized, the goods and material they had seized and wanted to bring over to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that is to cross from the Bosnian side of the bridge back into the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you did cross the bridge and stand foot in the Bosnian municipality of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe for us what you observed and what you did once you'd arrived in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As soon as I crossed the bridge, I saw a lot of people, mostly wearing civilian clothes, but armed. Some of them were wearing camouflage uniforms or combined army uniforms with, for example, one part army uniform and the rest in ordinary trousers or jeans or whatever, and not with army boots, but for the most part they were wearing ordinary civilian shoes or sneakers. And I knew that it wasn't the regular army and that like the man up over there who I described during the last session, that they were like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you described for us yesterday that the first time you were in Mali Zvornik, you could see Yugoslav army tanks in the Bosnian municipality of Zvornik. Could you see tanks there on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were tanks there and artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could you see whether those tanks and artillery pieces were manned by regular members of the Yugoslav army or by members of these paramilitary groups that you've just described for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the end of the bridge, edge of the bridge on the Bosnian side, there was a tank right up by the bridge itself, and in that tank there was a soldier, and he was coming out of the turret. You could see his head sticking out of the turret. And I exchanged a few words with him. I don't remember what we actually talked about, but we exchanged a few sentences not of any importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you asked one of the people on the street to direct you to whomever was in charge in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I asked several people, and I was told straight away, and I checked this out by asking others, they directed me towards the headquarters of the Territorial Defence in one of the streets in the centre of town itself. At least, I had the feeling that this was the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did they tell you the name of the person who was in charge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did they tell you his name was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They said it was a man called Marko Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did any of these people indicate to you whether he was a native of Zvornik or whether he was from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They told me that it was Major Marko Pavlovic. Nobody -- I asked, "Is he from these parts, from here? Is he from the Territorial Defence?" And they said, "No. He's a man who came here from somewhere else."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is this the same Marko Pavlovic who you later learned had another name, that is Branko Popovic, and who you later learned was associated with Mihalj Kertes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Branko Popovic, in fact. I learnt that his name was Branko Popovic, and he himself, several years after that, confirmed that when I talked to him in Sombor, because he was from the town of Sombor, and his name was in fact Branko Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you go and speak with this man on the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I went to see him in his office. There was some sort of security detail, some armed persons in front by way of security. I showed my journalist's ID card, and they let me go through. I went up some stairs and went into the office, introduced myself, and that's where we had our conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before I ask you about that conversation, I would ask you to describe for the Chamber the general appearance of the office. Did it have things such as maps and other types of equipment one might expect to find in a command centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't notice that. I don't know, actually. I don't remember. But it was an ordinary sort of office. It was no different from any other office in an administrative building, for example, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you please tell us in substance what you discussed with Major Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked him what was going on over there in Zvornik. He was rather upset, visibly afraid and concerned because, as he said to me just before that, he had had a problem. It consisted of the following: A certain leader of a certain paramilitary group, his nickname was Cele, that is the only thing that is known as far as he is concerned, and he came and he mistreated him at his office. He took out his pistol and he placed it against the man's head. That is what the man said to me, all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, so that it is clear, who put the gun against whose head? If you would please use the names just so that we're clear on what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cele came into the office of Marko Popovic or, rather, Marko Pavlovic, i.e., Branko Popovic, and he placed a pistol against his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did Cele belong to a particular paramilitary organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If it can be put that way, he was one of Seselj's men. This was one of Seselj's units.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did Major Pavlovic say what it was that Cele wanted from him? Why did he put the gun to his head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Cele thought - now, I don't know whether that's correct - that Major Pavlovic was also taking part in that, namely that Cele cannot cross the bridge with his men, with his booty, and with his weapons because there were Serb forces on the other side that did not allow the weapons and the booty to be carried in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did Major Pavlovic tell you about any phone calls he may have made regarding this situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He said to me that he had called Radmilo Bogdanovic and Seselj and that Seselj told him that Cele and his unit were out of control and that they had nothing to do with him. I don't know what he talked about with Bogdanovic. He didn't say that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it that he didn't tell you what Bogdanovic said to him or did he also not tell you what he said to Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. At that time, Bogdanovic was a retired person but still a person of considerable influence in the republican police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did Major Pavlovic tell you what he said to Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't tell me. He only said that he had called him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time that you left Major Pavlovic's office and encountered Cele himself on the streets of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Not far away from there, I encountered Cele who was accompanied by two young men who were also armed. He recognised me because it seems that we had seen each other before, in Borovo Selo or in some village around Borovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you describe your encounter with him at that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spotted them and they spotted me. We were walking towards each other, and we had to meet. Then he recognised me. He spread his arms out and he introduced me to his two men as "the greatest Serbian journalist."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I accepted this conversation. I spoke to him, although I did not really remember him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for us how he was dressed and what, if any, weapons he had with him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had ammunition belts with ammunition. He also had grenades at his belt. He was wearing a camouflage uniform. He also had a Serb cap, called sajkaca, with a cockade on it. He wore a beard. It was a pretty long beard. What I noticed was that he wasn't wearing leather shoes or trainers. He had a type of slippers on made of some kind of soft cloth. It looked like sneakers, but it wasn't really sneakers. That was quite strange because it didn't really fit into what else he was wearing. I assumed that he had some problems with his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you notice whether he had a knife with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He had a knife, a long kama, a double-edged knife, which is characteristic, because at the top there was a crown, top of the handle. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where was he carrying this knife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On his hip, on his belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you've just indicated with your hand your right side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was on the right side or on the left side, I can't remember any more, but it was on the hip. It was on his belt, as this is usually worn.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when Cele took you somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where did he take you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that we could go and have lunch together at a restaurant. All four of us got into a car - I know that it didn't have any licence plates - and we set out along the road, as I've shown on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the place that you indicate on the map where he took you is C4-3; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I had skipped that part, but before going -- or, rather, it was at the end that we went to this restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, the Judges have a copy of what you have before you, so I think at this point now, it would be sufficient if you just let us know the code name of how you indicated these different places.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He took me to where his unit was. This was the first time I ever saw this. I didn't even know that it existed before. It was like a big factory. Probably it was a factory. It was called Alhos.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time while at that factory that Cele took you to a room and showed you some property in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what he showed you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He showed me his medical team in a room where there were a few beds. There were lots of TV sets there, video recorders, also music players and all kinds of other equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you form an impression whether these were new TV sets and other electronic equipment or whether they were used pieces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first thing I realised and noticed was that none of this was new. All of it had been used. That was obvious. Also, it wasn't packed in the boxes the way these things come, but the TV sets and the video recorders were stacked like books.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he also take you to introduce you to some women that were present there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who did he indicate that these women were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said to me that that was the medical company, his medical company.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what did you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was supposed to understand that they were nurses. They didn't look like nurses. They were wearing mini skirts, short ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he describe a confrontation that he had with somebody regarding these women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After having introduced these nurses, he told me that Peja - that's Arkan's deputy who was also in Zvornik - while they were somewhere out in the field cleansing the field, he gathered them up, put them on a bus and transferred them across the Drina River to Serbian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you described two men by the name of Peja that were associated with Arkan. Were you able to ascertain which one of these two men Cele was referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the Peja who was nicknamed Ciganin, the Gypsy. I can't remember any longer exactly whether it was one or the other. I did not know them. I had heard about them but I did not really know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you left this headquarters building of Cele and go to another facility in the town of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He insisted that we go together to the brick factory, and that wasn't very clear to me, that is to say why we were going, but I did go.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you describe for us your observations once you arrived at the brick factory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They told me that in Zvornik, only the brick factory was still in operation. There were finished products there, rather, bricks, that were stacked up as usual at a brick factory, and he took me to see the manager, who was in his office. We talked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What ethnicity was the manager?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Obviously a Serb. He was introduced to me as the manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what, in substance, did the manager say to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the present day, I cannot -- I cannot understand what Cele did. He told me about some business deals and that this factory would be prosperous and contribute to the development of Zvornik as a town, as if he had an interest involved, a business interest. That is the only way in which I could interpret his interest in the brick factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Aside from the manager, were there any other workers around that you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. It's interesting that I didn't see any workers at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you recall what day of the week this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall which day it was, but later on, we established that it had been a Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is that by looking -- you were able to establish that by looking at a calendar from that year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, after you left the brick factory, did Cele take you somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After leaving the brick factory, we went to have that lunch that he said that we should go to. We went to this restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where was that restaurant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately, as far as I can remember, about four or five kilometres away from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was that travelling northward or southward?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This road. That is to say to the north, if the south is there. Or, rather, if the north is there and the south is down here, and this is the west, according to this map -- or, rather -- or, rather, this was downstream. This road also went by the Drina River, so it was down the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you mark the area where you were taken for lunch on that map as C4-5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the road. That's the road that goes there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is that area of Zvornik popularly known as?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe I knew before but I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How long did the lunch last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, several hours. I cannot establish the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for us some of the things that you discussed with Cele?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did most of the talking. He told me about the successes of his unit in, as he had put it, "cleansing the field." I had no idea then what this meant, "cleansing the area," the field. I understood that from what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ask him to tell you what he meant by "cleansing of the field"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. "Cleansing the field" means liberating it from the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did he describe for you an operation of such cleansing that he had participated in the night before, the 19th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He said to me that they were cleansing the field all night and that they did not fire a single bullet, but that they were working only with cold steel. I understood what he meant. And then when he said that, he used his hand to touch that knife. I have a very vivid memory of that. Then I asked him, "Was it everybody?" And I sort of showed children like this with my hands, and he said, "Yes, so that they would never return." That is something that you remember forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And for the record, you held out your hand about a metre off the ground. Is that what you did to indicate you were asking him what happened to the children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Like this. I meant children, and he understood it that way, yes. That meant that children were also killed the way he had put it to me, and that is how I understood it, because he said, "So that they would never return again."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You put, Mr. Groome, the 19th of May. I thought earlier the date of this visit to Zvornik was the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour. You are correct. I'll correct that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, your visit to Zvornik was indeed on the 10th of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's what it says in my diary -- in my notes, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So I was incorrect when I said the night before was the 19th. In fact, it was the 9th of May, is that correct, that he's describing this event to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the date really. I just know that above these notes it says the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before the lunch concluded, did Cele ask you to call several people on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He asked me whether I knew Vojislav Seselj. I said to him that I know him but that I don't know where he might be and how I could get in touch with him. Then he gave me some telephone numbers that I wrote down; the home telephone number and the office telephone number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to recall those telephone numbers as you sit here in court today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but I did have them at the moment when I talked about this before. I had the originals of all my notes, and all of this became part of the record, as far as I can remember. I cannot recall now. I never even tried to remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you record those numbers in your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that the witness be permitted to refresh his recollection as to those numbers by looking at his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I've opened up your statement to page 9. I'd ask you to look at the paragraphs towards the bottom of that page and ask you if that refreshes your recollection as to the numbers you were asked to call.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the office number of Vojislav Seselj?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was the home number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 848-3428. That is what he had dictated to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could have the statement back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, what was the message that Cele asked you to convey to Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I found in my writing pad said the following: "Pejo is after Cele to arrest him." That is what I had written down. And then it also said: "Five per cent of the population of Zvornik will join the Radical Party, and I await further instructions."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever call Mr. Seselj and pass on this message?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Whom else did he ask you to call?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember -- oh, yes. Yes. Yes. He also asked me whether I knew Zeljko Raznjatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that is Arkan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Arkan. And he also dictated to me what I was supposed to tell him. He said to me, "Pejo --" or, rather, "With all due respect" - he addresses him, "With all due respect" - "Pejo is working against the Serb cause."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you take this to mean the Pejo who you described as being an associate of Arkan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. One of his senior officers in the guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever pass that message on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time before you left the area of Zvornik and Mali Zvornik that you once again saw Major Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him again. I think it was several years later. I can't remember exactly in what year.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever see him again on the 10th of May, before you left Zvornik this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw him on the Serbian side in a cafe. It was called either Mali Zvornik or Mali Raj. I don't recall exactly what its name was, but it was the only cafe on the bank of the river. It was actually part of a hotel. I saw him in the evening, and he said that his family was being threatened somewhere, he didn't say where, and that he had to go to Belgrade urgently. As far as I know, he did go.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you had a conversation with some of the soldiers along the Drina regarding large birds that were flying in the sky on the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was with one of the people on the bridge, on the Serbian side. Eagles were flying around in large numbers, and I noticed that. I told him that, and he was a little -- I was a little surprised. And he said to me, "There have never been more corpses floating down the Drina River than there are now."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sometime later did you become aware of and set out to investigate a set of serious allegations regarding events in the area of Celopek in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I forgot to mention that I believe the man's name was Marko Pavlovic, but Cele then told me that that was not his real name and that he came from somewhere in Vojvodina. I was very interested in this, and then I heard, when I was writing about this topic, somebody rang me up and told me that Marko Pavlovic was in fact Branko Popovic and that he came from Sombor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is Sombor in Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Sombor is in Vojvodina, yes, yes. I managed to find out beyond any doubt by going to Sombor and interviewing Branko Popovic, alias Marko Pavlovic. Respectable people from Sombor told me that he was a member of the local State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to the events in Celopek. Did you as a journalist set out to investigate allegations that you became aware of of certain events in Celopek?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you give us a general description of the allegation that you were investigating.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I investigated a massacre of civilians in Celopek or, rather, in the local community centre which is by the roadside, along the road that leads to Celopek. The civilians who were inside were shot at, and it was Vuckovic, Dusan Vuckovic, also known as Repic, who killed -- I don't remember the exact number, but some 15 people and wounded about 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did -- are these the same Vuckovics that you referred to as being members of the Yellow Wasps yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vucko Vuckovic. Yes. Yes. His -- he was the elder brother of Vojin Vuckovic. His brother Vojin Vuckovic was the commander of the Yellow Wasps, and the other brother was called Dusan, also known as Repic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in the course of your own investigation into the events at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Celopek, did you cooperate in the production of a documentary of what happened in Celopek?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did make a documentary and interviewed the protagonists of these events. Well, not Dusan but his brother, the commander of the Yellow Wasps, Vojin Vuckovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you personally interview Vojin Vuckovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was a colleague of mine who did that, but it was a man we had worked with who was a filmmaker, as we say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you personally interview Vojislav Seselj in the creation of this documentary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you also interview a person by the name of Jose Mendiluce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, earlier this week were you asked to view a videotape of this documentary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that the witness be shown a videotape, just the physical cassette and not the playing of it, and it is marked as Prosecution Exhibit 342, tab 13, and the translation is in the binders. I would just ask that the witness be shown the actual video cassette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, he can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, is that the cassette that you looked at? And how do you know that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I marked it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you write the date that you looked at it and C-004 on that cassette?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to propose the following: I think it's probably more appropriate to view -- for the Chamber to view this videotape at the time we deal more specifically with Zvornik, but there is a 30-second or 40-second portion of the tape of an interview that Mr. Dulovic did with Mr. Seselj that is cued up and ready to be played now. I'd ask that this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's just examine the matter for the moment. The transcript which we have deals, I take it, with the entire video. Plainly, at this stage that is not admissible because it deals with comments by witnesses and that sort of thing which we wouldn't admit. But you're asking for the passage of the interview with Seselj to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's on page 14, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Page 14 of the transcript. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would ask the Chamber to consider the admission of the entire tape as an investigative documentary, produced by an independent organisation and person unrelated to the Office of the Prosecutor, realising that it may have less weight than the people who give interviews, but certainly there are some interviews which the Prosecution would argue should have some significant weight, namely that of Vojin Vuckovic, one of the perpetrators of the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we need to consider this, because we don't admit videos. We haven't so far admitted videos in which people describe what has happened, on the grounds that it's not the best evidence. I seem to remember several such instances. Plainly what somebody in the conspiracy or the joint enterprise mentions, such as Seselj, that could be -- that's admissible, and indeed if there are other admissions of crime, they may or may not be admissible. But at this stage, you want simply to introduce page 14, that passage; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And I think we would leave the admissibility of the rest of the video until we've heard further evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Can I make just one further point on that? This video also does show the areas involved. Can I lay a foundation with that with the witness? It may be of benefit to the Chamber at least to see the area of Celopek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, does the documentary also show Celopek, Zvornik, and other areas related to the crimes that occurred in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does it also contain some footage from Vukovar which you've testified and show the areas of Vukovar that you described yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I'd ask that that 40-second portion be played and that we view that and I'll ask the witness some questions afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: "Dulovic: Yesterday you said on television that Milosevic was the one who supplied the weapons to your men, that he participated actively in all of this and then just turned his back on you. "Seselj: Yes, that's a fact. [Interpretation] In 1991 and 1992 Milosevic was a leading nationalist and a patriot at that time we had close cooperation. When 30.000 paramilitary volunteers were sent to the fronts where Serbian people had to fight he was the one who supplied the arms, the ammunition, the clothes and the food, he provided the transportation, he allowed the use of military facilities and so on, and so on."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, the voice on the tape was a translator purportedly translating the statement made by Mr. Seselj. My question to you is: As the person who interviewed Mr. Seselj, was that an accurate translation -- or is that an accurate statement of what Mr. Seselj said when you interviewed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I interviewed Dr. Vojislav Seselj, I don't speak English, but this is what he told me, because this part referred to particular matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us approximately when it was you interviewed Dr. Seselj on this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the year. It's on the tape, the date when it was made. I think it might have been 1996, perhaps, but I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you put the question to Mr. Seselj regarding the supply of volunteers and paramilitaries, were you referring to the paramilitaries and volunteers that you had personally observed in Vukovar, Zvornik, and Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when Mr. Seselj said that Mr. Milosevic supplied 30.000 paramilitary volunteers with weapons and clothes and et cetera, did he at any time later in the interview say that that was an exaggeration or retract that statement in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, he didn't. While I was interviewing him, he didn't say that that was an exaggeration, nor did he ever deny what he had said, at least not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the period of time that Dr. Seselj alleged that he received this support from Mr. Milosevic was both in 1991 and in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So at least a portion of that support --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I only wish to say that this is a recording made in 1996. A few days ago, we discussed this extensively. I think no one can explain what somebody else meant to say, what somebody else thought. We discussed this several days ago, and you took up a position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's a matter for us to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So my question to you was: So at least a portion of the support that Mr. Seselj is referring to occurs after the urgent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, this is the point he makes: We can determine this. It's not really for the witness to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, I want to ask you a few questions regarding the role of the media and from your own experience as a journalist during this time, and I want to begin by asking you: During the course of the conflict, can you approximate for us how many stories or articles you submitted to Politika Ekspres per week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended on the situation and on the events that were taking place, but I tried to send a longish text or a piece of information every day. Whenever I was able to do so, whenever I had material, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in your view, was the reporting that you submitted, was it an accurate reflection of the events that you observed and interviewed people about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were all of your submissions printed or published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. Most of them were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Of the ones that were published, were any of the words that you had written, originally written, were they ever changed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you give us an example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For example, during the siege of Vukovar, I never used the word "Ustasha" or "bojovnik," meaning "soldier." I referred to the Croatian army and Croatian volunteers. What happened was that someone in a position of responsibility in the editor's office would change my words and use the expressions "Ustasha" and "bojovnik." I didn't like this, and I protested. I asked that this not be done any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was the -- what response did you receive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They said it wouldn't happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you -- and did it happen again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but then my stories were no longer printed at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when -- during a meeting of yourself and your editor-in-chief when your editor-in-chief received a phone call?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were all in the room where meetings were held and the phone rang. The editor-in-chief, Slobodan Jovanovic, spoke on the phone, and when he put down the receiver, he said that we had greetings from Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dulovic, you personally witnessed the JNA's entry into the town of Visegrad. Did there come a time after that that you were able to read and see the media coverage of that event?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, before that, could we get the date when Mr. Milosevic had called the editor-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, can you tell us, as best you're able, when that meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Meetings took place every day, so it's really impossible to remember the date. But the only thing I can say was that it was during the time when Slobodan Jovanovic was editor-in-chief of Politika Ekspres. Exactly when he was appointed and when he was dismissed, I don't know. I didn't feel it necessary to remember these dates, and I can't remember them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the year then? Do you remember the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not even the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you remember when -- when you left the employment of Politika Ekspres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in 1990 something. I don't know. I have a written document, but I don't recall the date. I don't have a good head for dates unless I write them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether this meeting occurred during the conflict or after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the conflict, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to return to the issue of Visegrad. Can you describe for us the press coverage and the media coverage of the JNA entry into Visegrad and express your opinion whether or not you felt it was accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was present when they entered Visegrad. There was no resistance, but the papers said that after hours of intensive fighting, the army entered Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was that just one or two papers or was that the general view of all of the newspapers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in all the state-sponsored newspapers, which were in the vast majority. There were hardly any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dulovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions of Mr. Dulovic at this time. In response to Your Honour's suggestion yesterday that we have a stock-taking, I propose just to state for the record the exhibits that I believe sufficient foundation has been established for, if that suits the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In Prosecution Exhibit 342, the Prosecution would tender all exhibits from 1 -- tab 1 to 13, subject to the limitations the Chamber has expressed on the record. And with respect to Prosecution Exhibit 343, that is the maps, the Prosecution would tender tabs 1 through 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will admit the 40 seconds of the video. The rest will simply be marked for identification, no more. I'm sure the registry could work out a way of doing that. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make one suggestion regarding maps, if I may? I expect during the course of the case, we'll be asking other witnesses to make marks on a copy of the same map. May I suggest that the maps that Mr. Dulovic marked on, that the suffix C4, his witness number, be added to that and that, when future witnesses testify, that their witness number be added as a suffix to the same tab -- tab number. Perhaps in that way, at the end of the case, all of the same maps will be in the same tab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we could do that or they could be given numbers. All right. Or the initials, the registrar recommends. But we'll keep them together in some way, which obviously is the important thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would Your Honour also like for the Prosecution to submit a blank copy of all photographs and maps so that the Chamber also has an unmarked version of all of these maps and documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we're all right, speaking for the Bench. We don't need any more. We've got them. Has the registry got a copy? They may have a view.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I only have copies of the marked. I would prefer to have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the registry have the clean copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn now, Mr. Dulovic. Could you be back, please, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I would like us first of all to clarify this question of a closed session for the cross-examination. The witness testified publicly all day yesterday, so it is my right, with respect to what he was testifying about yesterday publicly, to cross-examine him also publicly, because this is quite obviously a media operation, and I have emphasised on several occasions thus far that you are making -- you are working in a media environment and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not a legal environment. So if he was enabled to testify publicly yesterday throughout the whole day, I also have the right to cross-examine him publicly about the matters that he testified to yesterday. I will not be asking him, of course, in the public session of the cross-examination anything about what he testified today in today's closed session. We can leave that for a closed session, although some of the matters raised yesterday and today -- some of the matters he raised today were raised by him yesterday as well. But I would like to cross-examine him publicly only on his testimony yesterday, otherwise, we can't speak of any equality of arms between the two parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is what you call a legal environment. It is we who are the Judges who hear the evidence. As to whether the public hear it or not, that is a matter which may be subject to the security considerations which we've mentioned already, but we'll hear what the Prosecution have to say and then we'll allow the witness to address us on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's difficult to address you on it because I'm not sure what the witness's view is on it. May I have an opportunity to address you after we hear Mr. Dulovic's views? Of course, our primary concern is the security of his family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Dulovic, the accused is asking to cross-examine you in open session about those matters which were the subject of open-session evidence yesterday. Now, we have ordered that your evidence be heard in closed session because of the threats which have been made to your wife. The only reason could be for an open session are something to do with the public nature of the proceedings, but it is, of course, subject to security matters. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, on reflection, we're not going to ask you your views about the matter. We've come to the conclusion that this is a matter entirely for us. We're going to remain in closed session. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, in view of the fact that I would like to challenge everything that this witness has said, everything, I think that the interests of justice have been deeply harmed by your decision not to allow this to go public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we shall hear your challenge. And since it's we who are judging the case and nobody else, no harm is done to the interests of justice. Now, we've ruled on the matter. Now, would you like to begin your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, you are well aware of the fact that secret trials belong to the very distant past, and I have evoked that on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Milosevic, you should be aware of the seriousness of threats being made to the families of these witnesses. This Court will take very seriously its duties to protect its witnesses. Now, get on with the cross-examination and stop arguing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dulovic, you have behind you a long professional career as a journalist. Did you ever read that very lucid sentence of the famous German Otto von Bismarck who said the following: Lies are made most before voting, during a war, and after hunting"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a relevant question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think that what we have been hearing here for a day and a half shows just how relevant it is and how very true the quotation I stated a moment ago. Mr. Dulovic, you made two statements, one in October 2001 and one five years before that, in the month of May, 1996. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read something out from the first two or three pages of your statement of the year 2001, and then I'll go on to ask you some questions about that. Let's skip all this about when you met people from the OTP and so on, but you say: "At the beginning of August 2001 in Belgrade, an employee of the state security centre was killed, Momir Gavrilovic. He was a high-ranking official." And you go on to say that: "A lot was talked about in Serbia and it was said that the man had been killed because he went to President Kostunica and disclosed information with respect to the links between the State Security Service and the Mafia. I'm also deeply convinced that Gavrilovic was killed because he did recount to Kostunica some of the things about well-known Mafia people and their security with the -- and their links with the state security as well as the extent of the corruption that was involved. Later on, the minister, Minister Mihajlovic, he was Minister of the Interior, in a television programme, disclosed the names of some well-known criminals and their possible links to the State Security Service. And Minister Mihajlovic mentioned the following names: Sreten Lukic, Luka, from the Svezdera team; Ljubisa Buke, nicknamed Cume, the head of the so-called Surcin clan in Serbia. And in that same programme, the chief of police in Belgrade, Bosko Buha, and the head of the police station in Novi Sad, Knezevic, were mentioned as people having links to the Mafia. It was said that Kostunica went quite berserk when he saw the programme and all this was to be treated as highly confidential stuff. "Zoran Djindjic, the present Prime Minister, and his democratic party asked that a highly confidential note be sent to the Prosecution on the conversation between Kostunica and this man. Nothing was published before Mihajlovic disclosed the names. "In Belgrade, it is common knowledge that between Kostunica and Djindjic, there is a conflict going over the matter of state security and the ties with the Mafia as well as the ties between criminal endeavours and certain members of the government, and your -- you have in mind the present government. "At a meeting of Dos in the night between the 28th and 29th of August, 2001 went on throughout the night. I know that the subject of the meeting was the DB, the state security system, and the links with the Mafia and I do consider that this matter will be solved using political means. "For a certain amount of time after Gavrilovic was -- after Gavrilovic was killed, I realised that I had known him. I had met him in Croatia, in Vukovar, and one of the places that I met him was the centre for training in Erdut. At the time, he was there with Arkan. Momir Gavrilovic introduced himself as being a colonel of the JNA, Peric, and this happened after the fall of Vukovar. After Gavrilovic was killed, his photographs were published in the media and I recognised him straight away as the man who had introduced himself as being Colonel Peric. I learnt from reliable sources that members of the DB, the security service, worked as instructors and members of the Territorial Defence and paramilitary forces who were regularly not well trained. They were there to prevent chaos and to introduce law and order in the places where they worked as instructors," and so on and so forth. Then once again, at the end of page 2, you go on to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we must come to a question. I haven't stopped you yet, but you're supposed to be asking questions, not reading large parts of the statement. What is the question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have to read another portion before I can ask my question, because he goes on to say that: "There were links between the present members of the DB, the security service, with the Mafia, and they have a lot to answer for, and that people who know Zoran Djindjic, the present Prime Minister, says he uses 100.000 Deutschmarks a month on bodyguards and they're wondering who's paying for that. Everyone knows that Djindjic is into the cigarette smuggling business and that some rich people involved in the import business get preferential treatment from him in their day-to-day business. You used to say that you think that Zoran Djindjic is a dangerous person," et cetera, et cetera. And then you say: "If you ask me about the fear of a military putsch, my answer to you would be that I'm not afraid of that, I think the army has no one strong enough to be in charge of any coup. Personally, I am at war with the army leadership and I would describe the present chief, Pavkovic, as a pompous little person, pompous little man."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, all this is about current politics. None of it has, as far as I can see, any bearing on the indictment. Now, could you please ask a relevant question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's just what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What has this to do with me, and what has this to do with your testimony, and is it quite clear that the party over there, the opposite party, is involved in political intrigue, using observations of this kind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a matter for the witness as to what the Prosecution are involved in or not. But the fact is that none of this is relevant to the trial. Now, if you want to ask a question that's relevant, of course, about it, you can, but it's not a matter which we shall take account of. If you want to ask the witness why it's in the statement, you can do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's precisely what I'm asking him, Mr. May, what all this is about. Is it quite clear that what we're dealing with here are political manipulations and not a trial, in fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a proper question. Mr. Dulovic, you heard the passages read out by the accused, and his question is: How do they come to be in the statement? Can you help us as to that, since they appear to have absolutely nothing to do with this particular trial. Can you help us or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was what I was saying, and I had the impression that the Prosecution was interested in these things, and I recounted the things I had heard, what I thought about them, and so on. Now, whether they have anything to do with this question in hand, it's not for me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, do you believe that it is precisely journalists who very often create events themselves for the eyes of the public on the basis of their impressions and sometimes on the basis of their political options too? At other times, it would be perhaps because of interest, through their own interests, and sometimes it is to the detriment of the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your previous colleague, Mr. Anastasijevic, also works for the same paper, for the magazine Vreme. Do you know that in our country there is the widespread conviction that that magazine of yours is an extended arm of the services which in fact worked against Yugoslavia, and the editorial staff of the Vreme magazine, to all intents and purposes, is the only editorial office which endeavours to show the Serbs as being wholly responsible for the war and thereby confirming that it is working for the services working against Yugoslavia? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know -- do you think that one can say you are an impartial witness when you describe these events? Could you be characterised that way in your descriptions of what happened in the former Yugoslavia and your testimony here in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, is it quite clear, then, that you, in your testimony, refer to the talks you had and interviews and who told you what? You refer to these all the time, so that the bulk of your testimony is not testimony as to fact but testimony about what you heard from others and on the basis of what your political positions are. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're not testifying about what you heard from others. Everything you have described to us, you say, "This person told me that," "I had lunch with so-and-so," "I talked with so-and-so," "I was sitting around with 10 people and one of them said such-and-such." You keep telling us what other people told you. But did you personally see a killing take place? Did you personally see one of the crimes perpetrated that you described all day yesterday here and today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Dulovic, that you were an associate of the State Security Service or, rather, that you were in cahoots with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that when you visited the battleground and collected up the Zolja type of weapon, that you yourself said that you didn't know how many Zoljas you had in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is absolutely not true. It's nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, were you ever in prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were never arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody prevent you from carrying out your duties as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember. Ask me specifically what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I mean on the whole. You worked as a journalist. Did anybody hinder you, from the authorities or anybody? Did anybody hinder the performance of your journalistic duties? Did you have any negative consequences on the basis of what you did as a journalist, at the papers you worked at or where you work now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, only what was important to all journalists and which is the only thing that could be a hindrance, that is closing off important channels of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand this very well. What was the point of the explanation you gave towards the end of the examination-in-chief today, that I spoke on the telephone to Slobodan Jovanovic, your editor-in-chief? You said that this was after the conflict, et cetera. So what's this all about? I assume that you remember that Slobodan Jovanovic was a high official of the Socialist Party of Serbia. For a while he was even Chairman of the City Committee of the party in Belgrade. So what? Did he say something to you to the effect that I had intervened as to what the paper should write or something like that, or are you simply stating that I had a telephone conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that you were in close touch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of that telephone conversation, it is your assessment I was in close touch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only that. On the basis of the fact that at the eighth session of the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Serbia, he was one of those who strongly supported you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did say that he was a high official of the Socialist Party of Serbia at the time that we were discussing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you objecting to something he did, that he committed a crime or that he did something wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he did something wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what is this wrong thing he did, improper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He let all kinds of nonsensical lies into -- be published in the newspapers. For example, that in the village of Mirkovci a barrel full of eyes was found, Serb eyes, and that Ustashas were making pies out of them; things like that. That kind of propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for propaganda, you probably know that the main propaganda was carried out by opposition newspapers whereas the state-controlled media tried to act in a very moderate fashion, although all of you wrote Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. whatever came to your minds. Tell me, please, since in your statement you mention events in Vukovar, your stay, and as you said, the impermissible behaviour or violence -- actually, do you think that an event can be viewed in an isolated manner outside the general context of events, as you do in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is only one of the examples involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, I assume that you know full well that there is no war that is worse than a civil war and that nothing can be corrected in that respect. Only those who care for the good can do their best to have the war stopped altogether, not to have things merely corrected. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that Serbia's policy throughout the time was that this war should be brought to an end at all costs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a lie, an ordinary lie, because Serbia was waging a war, or, rather, you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, don't you know that Serbia was not at war with Croatia or Bosnia-Herzegovina? A short while ago, you gave evidence about our police not allowing anyone to enter the territory of Serbia with weapons, across the Drina River. That's the example that you gave. So if that were true, if these were people who were sent by Serbia, then it would probably be possible for them to enter Serbia. Is that logical to you or is it not logical to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that already in May 1991 you travelled in Slavonia and that you saw many places there that the army was getting there in larger and larger numbers. Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As a journalist, did you find out anything about the enormous pressures that were brought to bear against the JNA throughout the territory of Croatia, about attacks against military barracks, the killings of soldiers, practically making it impossible to observe any kind of agreement that would bring the violence to an end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, in your statement you mention some kind of Vojna Linija in the Ministry of the Interior. You say that in this Vojna Linija of the Ministry of the Interior where Zivota Panic, Mihalj Kertes, Jovica Stanisic, Franko Simatovic, Radmilo Bogdanovic, Radovan Stojicic Badza, that's what it says here on page 2 of your first statement, and that that was established in 1990. And then yesterday -- well, the first page is the second page, sir. Mr. Dulovic, I see that you are looking at the second page. I often make the same mistake, because the first page here is the cover page, actually, and then the text starts with the second page where it says "Witness statement" in the middle and then further on. It was said that it was established in 1990, the Vojna Linija, and then all these names I mentioned. Now, could you please explain the following to me: Yesterday when you were questioned about the Vojna Linija, you gave the following explanation, that these were people who would graduate from the military academy while being members of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A small number of MUP members indeed did graduate from the military academy, but very few of them. For the most part, the highest positions were held by people who had a degree in law or social sciences, but this Vojna Linija of the Ministry of the Interior, let's see who this is. Zivota Panic, a general. He never worked in the MUP nor was he ever linked to the MUP. He was in the army all the time and he was even chief of staff for a while and, after that, he retired. Mihalj Kertes also did not graduate from any kind of military academy. He's a social worker. Jovica Stanisic, who was head of the State Security Service of Serbia for the longest period of time, did not graduate from any military academy. Franko Simatovic also. Bogdanovic also did not graduate from any military academy. Radovan Stojicic also. So none of them actually fall under the explanation that you provided yesterday, people who graduated from the military academy and worked at the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior. So what you say is incorrect; isn't right, Mr. Dulovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You misunderstood this. Yesterday I talked about people who were in the field, and I was told that this was the top leadership, and I pointed that out, that that is what I heard from a man who should know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you heard this from a man who should know about this, the question always arises as to whether this man does actually know, and secondly, whether this man speaks the truth, and thirdly, whether you are saying the truth as to whether you've heard it or not. So there are a few question marks involved before such a statement can be made or, rather, before this kind of evidence can be taken into consideration. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who is the man you heard this from, Mr. Dulovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't want to say his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Because this is an absolute falsehood. Could you explain to me how they operated? Because if you say there was this Vojna Linija, how did it operate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you are just making a broad-based statement that it did exist. Do you know that, at that time, the republics - and also later - the republics did not have any jurisdiction over the Yugoslav People's Army or could they have had any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Dulovic, you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Milosevic. I'm asking the interpreters whether it's possible to translate "Vojna Linija."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Vojna Linija" literally means "military line."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Military line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that that's the interpretation that the interpreters gave. I didn't look at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that in July and August 1991, you were in Borovo Selo, a suburb of Vukovar, and you say that you visited a prison there, and you describe what a guard demonstrated to you, that when he would bang at the door, that they would sing, sing the song "Who is saying, who is lying," et cetera, and then this other song dedicated to Vojvoda Sindjelic. Does it seem to you that this kind of an anecdote could not even be recounted in a pub in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, this is not an anecdote; this is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
