utterances.text: No. This is what I saw, this is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This had to be seen or heard by somebody else too in addition to yourself, if such things did exist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, many did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you mention anybody else who saw this or heard this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know any names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, then, although I do not believe what you're saying at all: Did you see near that prison any soldier of the JNA or, for example, a policeman from Serbia, Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How long were you in Borovo Selo? Do you actually know what happened in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about things. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As a journalist who stayed in Borovo Selo, did you establish what the then Minister of the Interior of Croatia, Josip Boljkovac ascertained and which was later admitted, seven years later, in December 1998, that bloodshed in Borovo Selo was caused by the members of the MUP of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that Boljkovac himself said that members of the Croatian MUP entered Borovo Selo, caused a conflict, took the flag down, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this same Minister of the Interior of Croatia, Boljkovac, said that the mortar attack on Borovo Selo that was commanded by Gojko Susak and Vice Vukojevic, Ivica Vukojevic were a call to war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know about that either. Do you know the statement that the aim of this attack was to render impossible the peaceful break-up of Yugoslavia, also that this was not a mere incident but an action prepared --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said he doesn't know about it, so there's no point going on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what I'm asking him about, I mean, he is a journalist and he is interested in this. This was published in a special edition of Croatian Globus on the 18th of May, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can produce it to us in due course, but the witness -- there's no point asking the witness about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, since the witness is giving evidence about only a fraction of these events and he is taking this out of the context of these horrors of Vukovar, I am trying to establish whether he is aware of the origins of the conflict, whether he knows how they started, what the intensity was, and how many victims were the result of this, in order to clarify the role of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why don't you ask him asking else, then? There's no point asking something about which he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, during your stay in Vukovar, in Borovo Selo, for example, or generally in that area, did you come to the conclusion that the HDZ was being armed, that is to say the ruling party in Croatia? Not only did they get weapons but also dynamite in order to blow up Serb houses, business facilities that were owned by Serbs. For example, precisely in Borovo Selo where you were, they blew up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness -- let the witness deal with the general question first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't there at the time, nor did I see the members of the HDZ, so I don't know anything about what the accused is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you didn't see many of the things you testified about but only heard about then. Did you know that the restaurant Sarajica, owned by a Serb from Borovo Selo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- was blown up by the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you avoided using the term "Ustasha." Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the perpetrators of crimes in the surroundings of Vukovar, and of course elsewhere, called themselves Ustasha? They referred to themselves as Ustasha and were proud of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't hear about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You explain that in September, October, and November 1991, the shelling of Vukovar did not stop. How long were you in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, almost throughout the entire three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how the conflict in Vukovar came about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't there when it broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that first a decision was made on the ethnic cleansing of Vukovar in February 1991 at the meeting of the HDZ branch for Trpinje Cesta in Borovo Naselje? Did you hear about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about Mercep, Vekic [phoen], Seks who organised this entire pogrom activity on the territory of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The names are familiar to me but not in a context I could connect with this. I only heard the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Are you aware, then, that following the policy then adopted by Zagreb they issued decisions to have all Serbs dismissed from leading posts in the area, that they should be intimidated, made to leave, and those who did not do what was required would be liquidated? Do you know about these conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that as early as February 1991, the HDZ branch for Borovo Naselje set up several branches in the local communes and that in March 1991, for example -- I have precise information: On the 10th of March in the Bratstvo and Jedinsko local commune, which is what this was called, now it's called the Alojzije Stepinac hall, that a meeting was held of that Borovo Naselje branch and it was this that they discussed, the expulsion and liquidation of the Serbs. Are you aware of any of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this. There's no point asking this witness these questions. He knows nothing about it. It doesn't add to the case in any way. Mr. Milosevic, you've been told, in due course if you want to call evidence about these things, you can, but we're wasting time in cross-examination by this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope, Mr. May, that you will give me at least as much time for cross-examination as this witness of yours has had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know anything about the review of the future paramilitary formations of the Republic of Croatia in March 1991, precisely in this area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop these questions. Do you know -- Mr. Dulovic, can you help us at all about what the Croats were doing, whether there were meetings of this sort, or anything at all in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know nothing of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the ethnic cleansing of Borovo Naselje which then spread to other parts of the Vukovar municipality? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you wrote about Vukovar, you mentioned the hospital. Do you know that Dr. Rade Popovic, the head of the hospital, was dismissed and Vesna Bosanac was appointed in his place? Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only know Vesna Bosanac. I know she was the head of the hospital. I didn't hear about the other name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it seem abnormal to you that you know nothing about the enormous pogrom against the Serbs and the attacks in the army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a matter of comment. This is all your case that there was a pogrom. Nobody else has said so. So to put it to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witness as a criticism that he knows nothing about it is absurd. Now, could you just deal with questions which the witness can deal with. It may be you want to go on to the hospital and what the witness said he saw happening there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll come to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you know anything about the fact that a large part of the Croatian population, primarily women, children, civilians, and so on, were evacuated from Vukovar but the Serbs were not allowed to leave the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what was done before, but there were a lot of civilians, Croats, in Vukovar who were in the shelters together with the Serbs. I know about this because the Serbs who were in these cellars, in these shelters, told me this. They had been there together with the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you like to see the certificate issued by the Republic of Croatia, Vukovar municipality, Municipal Secretariat for National Defence, and then there is a seal with the chequerboard symbol and signature allowing Petar Kordo to leave the town and go from Vukovar in the direction of Osijek and Zupanja? So this is a permit. Without a written permit of the Croatian authorities, a civilian could not leave Vukovar if he was a Serb. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm hearing this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, please have a look at this permit, and I would like to tender it into evidence. I can give you several more of these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the usher get the document. Mr. Milosevic, I doubt the witness can say very much more than he's said already, that he heard from the Serbs that there were Croats in the -- in the town. But by all means let the witness have a look at it. Yes, to the Prosecution. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, since you were there on the spot at the time, that the top military command of the -- of Yugoslavia said that Croatia had done everything it had planned by then, had perpetrated crimes and mass persecutions of the Serbs in order to take Vukovar and its surroundings? I assume that you were keeping up with events then because you were already there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember this. All I know is what I saw, what I talked about with people. I know that in the shelters there were Serbs and Croats together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Are you aware of the fact that until the beginning of the fighting for Vukovar, before the fighting began, several thousand -- up to a thousand Serbs were killed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never heard this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I assume that it's common knowledge that on the 26th of July 1991, only a month before the decision on the secession of Croatia, the president of Croatia, Tudjman, issued a decree disbanding the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were many more Serbs living in that municipality in comparison to the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what the proportion was, but I know that there were both Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the HDZ, the party of the then President Tudjman, at the first multi-party elections in Croatia lost? They were badly beaten in Vukovar because the citizens in the area voted for the League of Communists of Croatia and the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't remember that? Do you know that the dissolution of the Assembly and the pressure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We're going to confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, may I assist you to reach a decision which of course it is for you to make? Why is all this important? In the statement he gave to the OTP, in paragraph 2, the witness said that: "From May 1991 onwards, in company with two other colleagues, I travelled around the towns and villages in Eastern Slavonia, watching the developments unfolding as the country approached the war." And he spent the following several months in the area constantly. So the questions that were put concern events in the area, in these towns and villages which the witness was constantly visiting and observing. And it is for you, of course, to decide whether the questions that were put are admissible. How is it possible that the witness does not know anything about all these events?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You can have the same time as the Prosecution; it will be four hours and a quarter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That means until the middle of tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll see how the time goes, but that's the time you can have. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. May, I am trying to show that it is incredible that the witness claims to have very good knowledge of certain crimes perpetrated by Serbs afterwards but that he knows absolutely nothing about the events that preceded this and gave rise to the conflict, the violence, the murder. A thousand people were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his answer. I expect what you say is contentious, it isn't accepted anyway by the Prosecution. We might get the Prosecution, actually, to shorten this. What we might do is, so it's not put to every witness that there was this referendum, there was this and that, we might get some agreed facts on what the -- if you can agree, some of the facts that the accused keeps putting to people, to save a bit of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just observe in respect of that, we still have very limited, if any, contact with his associates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I know that. I'm meaning on the basis of what's been put to witnesses already. I don't know if there's some facts you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can give thought to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- you can extract out of it so that we don't get every witness being asked if they know about this referendum or that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll give thought to it, but once things are raised a certain number of times, the Chamber may just decide that they just don't need to be raised again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it would help if they could be agreed so we knew they didn't have to be raised again. The other matter - it's a pity this isn't in open session because it's an important point - there may be matters which you can agree, from what the accused is putting, the more tendentious matters, that maybe some can be agreed, some can't, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll give thought to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, give some thought to it in order to save time. Mr. Milosevic, I'm saying to the Prosecution there may be some matters which you're putting to witnesses which can agreed by them so you don't have to keep putting it to these witnesses, but go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. May, I didn't put any questions -- I haven't put any questions so far about the conflicts to the witnesses. Vukovar. As I said, I have not previously put any questions regarding Vukovar to other witnesses, nor did I ask this witness about issues concerning the referendum and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So as you have just said, you have heard of Tomislav Mercep who perpetrated enormous crimes while leading these units. Of course you know nothing about these crimes, but do you know about the crimes that were committed in Vukovar immediately before these events, by the 204th Brigade of the National Guard Corps under the command of Mercep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you didn't see anything of what you're testifying about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. The question is did you hear about any crimes committed by this group? We don't know if there were or not, but it may be you can help us. Let the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Put it this way: Were there allegations about this group committing crimes, or indeed any other Croats, committing crimes in Vukovar before the -- before the siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can recall, I remember these names. I remember them in a negative context. There were stories and allegations that crimes were committed, but I had no relevant or valid evidence about this. Most probably these things did exist, but I did not go back in time when I arrived. I started reporting on what I saw and heard. I did not go into previous events after I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since these were events that certainly attracted enormous attention because of their cruelty, I have here a statement made by Marin Vidic Bili, an authorised representative of the Croatian government for Vukovar. It's 52 pages long, and I will read only half a page to you and then you can tell me whether you ever heard anything about this. His statement is 52 pages long, and I will tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, you won't tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As I see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can call him. You can call him to give evidence, if you want, but you can't simply put a statement in like that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But simply listen to what the authorised Croatian representative for Vukovar said in late 1991. This is 52 pages long. He says the following, this is on page 30: "The action against Borovo Naselje was carried out in early July. I cannot say exactly on what day. Apart from the fact that I knew the action would take place, we were informed by Zadro Blago, who led the action, as to how it was to take place. I was in the Secretariat for National Defence, under Mercep Tomislav, who contacted with Blago Zadro by way of a Motorola. Blago Zadro came to the secretariat at around 2200 hours. He informed us that the action in Borovo Naselje had been very successful, that there had been no wounded or killed members of the Ministry of the Interior and the guard, that Borovo Naselje had been cleansed of the Serbian population and the Chetniks and that in the cornfields behind it, the last row of houses of Borovo Naselje, in the direction of Borovo Selo, that there about 50 Chetniks had been killed as we were informed by Blago Zadro. The chief of the police administration was also present and he also confirmed this. I sent a report to the Crisis Staff in Osijek, and I gave the information that had been given to me by Blago Zadro. I know that Tomislav Mercep sent a report to the Crisis Staff in Zagreb, to its chairperson, Josip Manolic. He was then the Minister of the Interior. However, Mercep made a statement for the public in which he said that the Chetniks had attacked Borovo Naselje and that this had been successfully opposed by the guards and the members of the Ministry of the Interior and that they had driven out the Chetniks from Borovo Naselje and broken up their ranks. Tomislav Mercep's statement was broadcast by Croatian television and the aim of this was to inform the public --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to stop this because it's absolutely pointless asking this witness something as long as this, particularly as he may or may not know anything about it. Can you help us as to this allegation about an attack on Borovo Naselje? Do you know anything about this attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about that. I was a journalist who was following daily events. I wasn't writing stories and articles about things that had happened in the past or forecast the future. I was just giving the actual state of affairs of what was going on in the theatre of operations at the time I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, these are quite legitimate questions, because in your statement, you yourself say that the Serbs were doing the attacking and that the Croats were defending themselves. That's how you explain it. And then you give a completely distorted picture of the situation. This is a statement of their representative. It's 52 pages long.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you don't want to accept this, Mr. May, that's up to you, but I'm offering it up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not at the moment. If in due course it becomes admissible, we'll rule on it, but we don't accept statements unless there's good reason to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And would you like -- all right. Very well. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But would you like to comment on a document? You haven't got the document, of course, but from the aspects of your testimony, this is an official letter sent on the 18th of August, 1991, to the president of the Republic of Croatia, to the Prime Minister of Croatia, the Defence Minister, the minister in the Ministry of the Interior, and copies were sent to four addressees, the presidents of four parliamentary parties in the Croatian Sabor or parliament, the SDB among them, of Ivica Racak, the Prime Minister now, Sabkadacevic [phoen] Kuca, the president of the HNS, the HLS, Budisa and the HDS Veselica, and it was signed and stamped by a representative of the Republic of Croatia in the Vukovar municipality, Marin Vidic Bili. It has a stamp, it has a signature and all the rest, and this is what it says. It is titled "The Political Security in the Vukovar municipality, Report." "The nomination of Tomislav Mercep as secretary of the municipal secretariat in Vukovar came -- led to the usurping of power and focusing it in one person, in the person of the HDZ representative and therefore, the commander, to all practical purposes of the ZNG, the police and the organs of power and authority. He has surrounded himself by dubious people, former criminals, and by that they have taken over control of everyone in the municipality of Vukovar and they stop at nothing, repressive measures," et cetera, in the municipality. Then he goes on to state the measures that they have adopted; the unlawful storming of an apartments, looting, taking away vehicles, detaining people brutally, and this goes on as far as executions and liquidations. This is something that he writes about in this report. He is informing all the organs at the top echelons of Croatia, and says that this has led to a feeling of general fear among the Serbian and Croatian population, and there is a general exodus from the town, a blockade of the police, the ZNG, the organs of power and authority and has led to a general situation of confusion. And then it goes to say that Tomislav Mercep, upon the intervention of the minister from Zagreb, was withdrawn and dismissed as Minister of the Interior, and this was made public in the information media. And then he goes on to say later on that in addition to this, the head of the ZNG, Hipa [phoen] Radas, was replaced. He was a professional. And Mercep's deputy was brought in to replace him. And he goes on to say that: "A blockade was set up, that there was no work going on, there was great confusion, great fear among the population prevailed, and that the entire Croatian population did not justify this kind of conduct and thought that it had been compromised and that mud had been thrown upon it and it wishes to bear no responsibility for policies of this kind. As we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. consider that we are not able to clear up the situation with the use of local forces, would you please send competent people into the area urgently." So it is their representative who speaks about what Mercep's Ustashas were doing in Vukovar, the executions that were going on, the arrests that were taking place, and the way in which they ran amok. We see that 50 people were killed. They are referred to as Chetniks for the mere reason of being Serbs, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've been speaking now for several minutes and it's time there was a question. This has been put to you, Mr. Dulovic. Do you know anything about this letter or indeed about the situation which it describes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I hear of it. While I was over there while it was still under siege, I heard that in Vukovar that among the Croats there, there were certain rifts going on and conflicts and clashes of opinion, but I really don't know any more about the situation than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, I didn't ask you about the letter itself. I was interested in hearing from you, as the letter was an official one from official Croatian organs sent to the Croatian government and speaks about events, I'm asking you whether you knew anything about those events and that violence en masse and the killing of Serbs in Vukovar in the summer months of 1991. Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you know nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because Borovo Naselje was under Croatian jurisdiction. There was an airport, and then you get to Borovo Naselje. So I don't know what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, in view of the statements that I quoted and the generally known facts about the violence, can you really say what you said yesterday during your testimony, that the Serbs from Vukovar, after the fall of Vukovar, as thousands of them had been killed up until that date, looted and everything else destroyed, that you said that the Croatian authorities' conduct towards them was quite proper and that they had no criticisms to make in that regard and they had no criticisms vis-a-vis everything that was going on, and you claim that it was the Serbs from Vukovar who actually told you that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I'm saying. I have their names, their first and last names, their addresses noted down, and they told me what I recounted yesterday during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. These seem to be some very strange people, or perhaps what I have just quoted was incorrect, and I quoted Croatian sources at that. All right, then. Tell me this: Were you ever in the Petrova Gora Local Community in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That's on the other side of town from where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But when you arrived in Vukovar, I assume that you moved around throughout the whole town. I don't know which parts you visited, but that's why I'm asking you. Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you learn, perhaps later on, that in Vukovar within the frameworks of the Mercep brigade was the first group that was set up for these liquidations? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if that is so, then this took place on both sides, on the Serbian side and on the Croatian side. There was talk of the fact that on both sides these teams or groups were being set up, or units, for purposes of liquidation, and a lot of manipulation was done with rumours of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Dulovic. I quite understand the position you're in. Now, do you know that the first person to fall casualty, to fall victim to the Mercep group was Zeljko Ostojic, who at the end of 1990 testified to the organs of the security of the Yugoslav army about the formation of armed units and the plans of Tomislav Mercep for the ethnic cleansing of Eastern Slavonia? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you spent such a long time in Vukovar, do you know that after a film about Spegelj was broadcast over television, and he testified about that, so right after the programme was televised, Ostojic was killed in his apartment in Borovo Naselje because of that testimony, quite obviously. Did you ever learn about any of that? Hear about any of that? Nobody told you anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're saying that throughout your stay in Vukovar, none of the Serb population ever complained to you of the terror and killings that had been going on for months in Vukovar but that, as you yourself claim here, that all they said was that some mad Serbs were attacking Croats who were just defending themselves. That is your thesis, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I am saying that there was fighting going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And how about this: Do you know what the intention of the army was? Do you know anything about the blocking of the barracks in Vukovar? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me, please, what did you hear about it? The blockade set up in front of the barracks in the centre of Vukovar, what did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That it had been surrounded by the Croatian army, that there was fighting, and that the forces -- the soldiers managed to pull out of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement where you say you were called to be a witness, and the statement has been tendered here along with your statement, it is the records on witness interview -- witness interview that was conducted, in the documents that I was given from that opposite party there, you say: "I was present during the military activities of the JNA to deblock the barracks in Vukovar, or, rather, the action and operation, in inverted commas, you say of the liberation of Vukovar as it was called." That is in inverted commas. And then you go on to say the following, where you lived, where you resided, and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to take a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. It's 0288148. It is your own statement, at the beginning of your own statement, and you quoted from that statement as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe Mr. Milosevic is referring to tab 12. That's in evidence as Prosecution Exhibit 323. I would ask that the witness be shown that. And I apologise; for the record, it's 342.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 12?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the statement made to the investigative judge, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It appears that is the document Mr. Milosevic is quoting from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Has the witness got it? Tab 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Dulovic, if we bear in mind everything that was going on during that summer and the thousands of Serbs that had been killed up to that time, and when we bear in mind what you yourself call the blockade and deblocking of the Vukovar barracks, do you really think that the army should not have saved not only its own soldiers in Vukovar but also other citizens whose lives were in peril from one day to the next and who disappeared in the rampage the Ustasha groups engaged in, and these people called themselves Ustashas themselves, and we will be able to ascertain that in due course. Do you really think they should not have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must come to a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is do you think that the army should not have intervened to deblock the barracks and to stop the slaughter of civilians in Vukovar and 1.000 had already been killed up until that time? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If this were true, did you know anything about what is alleged here? This is the accused's allegations, of course, that there was a slaughter of civilians. I take it to mean a slaughter of Serb civilians. Did you hear anything of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, are you saying 1.000 Serbs had been killed? If I understand you correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, according to the facts and figures that I have. Up until that time, right after the proclamation of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That all took place during the summer of 1991, and everything happened much before the attack on Vukovar. The barracks were blocked in Vukovar far before the attack on Vukovar took place. Electricity was cut off, water was cut off, and the barracks were shot at from all sides in order to show that Croatian independence can be gained through a war, although the army, the soldiers wished to leave the barracks, but this was made impossible. And this witness must have known about all that. He knows -- he says he knows nothing about that, and there is an enormous amount of evidence and proof of that, and I myself have quoted a few.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed or would you like to take a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Quite right. It's break time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say one thing before the break? As it appears we may continue on until tomorrow, the Prosecution is concerned about this very serious security consideration and is asking the Chamber to consider making inquiry from the Victims and Witnesses Unit if it's something they feel that they are competent to investigate, and if they feel they are not, perhaps there would be an alternative where an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor could speak to Mr. Dulovic in the presence of either the registry or the amici. I would hate to lose valuable time in getting to the bottom of the extent of the threat that Mr. Dulovic's family is facing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll consider that during the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, dealing with the matter you raised before the adjournment, we will permit an investigator to speak to the witness about the matter. Of course he can only speak about what happened overnight, of course, not about the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, we said earlier on that you mustn't speak to anybody, of course, about your evidence, but because of the events involving your wife, we're going to permit an investigator to speak to you about that. If you would keep the conversation just to that, of course, not talking about your evidence or the case, but he can speak to you about that limited purpose. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you're a journalist, Mr. Dulovic, did you follow what was going on with the media at the time in Vukovar? Do you know, for example, that on the 2nd of May in this general pogrom atmosphere in Vukovar, the HDZ forcibly took over radio Vukovar and appointed Zdravko Seremet, member of the Municipal Council of the HDZ, to be the new director of radio Vukovar? Since this concerns your colleagues, other journalists, did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When I was there, Radio Vukovar was in the hands of the Serbs. There were two women journalists and one man there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about what happened beforehand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know nothing about that. Do you know that, on the same day, that is to say on the 2nd of May, there was a coordinated action of the MUP of Croatia engaged in the ethnic cleansing in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, for example, of the fact that a Croat, the chief of police of Croatia in Osijek, his name was Kir Reihl, who was energetically opposed against such Ustasha rampages in Vukovar, was killed on the Osijek-Vukovar road by these same men of Mercep's because he wanted to calm the situation down, because he wanted such operations to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know about that. I read about that and heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So if it is so, that is to say that they were killing their own chiefs of police who opposed such rampages, can you assume what the proportions of these rampages were and the level of endangerment of the Serb population that went on throughout the summer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot present any assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in October and November 1991, when you say that Vukovar was shelled all the time, that one-third of the total Croatian forces, together with foreign mercenaries - and we saw some of them here in a film - attacked Serbs in the area of Vukovar, precisely at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of this, especially about the foreign mercenaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in town itself at that time there was between 6.000 and 8.000 of these paramilitary formations of Croatia? They themselves called themselves Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you don't know about these groups, do you know that the basis for these forces at that time - I don't want to use the word Croatian forces because this, in a way, would smear the name of the Croatian people, but this was done by the 204th Vukovar Brigade, the brigade from Vinkovci, the brigade from Zagreb, 100 volunteers, 50 members of the MUP from Varazdin, Cakovec, 400 mobilised members of the guard corps, forces of the HOS unknown to me - that is to say HOS Croatian defence forces - and then these international mercenaries in the groups called Kondor, Chicago, 150 neo-fascists and mercenaries. Did you find out about this at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not find out anything about that. Either I or my colleagues. This is the first time I hear about this. Perhaps this was the case, but this is the first time I ever hear of it. These precise figures are something that journalists and ordinary people did not know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know or did you hear later that, Dogriv Kiso [phoen], Aleksandar Volter, Petar Binder, who were arrested in Austria, that is to say not in Eastern Slavonia or in Serbia but in Austria, towards the end of 1993, that they disclosed their own participation in that war, these neo-fascists, mercenaries? That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know about that either. All right. But I assume that it is not even being contested by you that when in October 1991 the army set out to Vukovar, that their task was to deblockade the barracks. Is that something that is not being contested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that was still operating and the JNA that was throughout the territory of the country, they even asked the European Community to mediate so that this deblockade could be carried out and so that the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. slaughters could be stopped? Only after the situation was quite clear that nothing would come out of that, it is only then that the army launched this attack in order to deblockade the barracks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't know anything about that. Newspapers did not arrive in Vukovar. For the most part, there was no electricity either. So I did not have the opportunity of hearing about this, even if it was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, do you know about the all-out attack of the MUP of Croatia and the National Guard Corps and other paramilitary formations against all blocked military barracks throughout the territory of Croatia? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I know about Slovenia. As for these, I don't know. Oh. I know, I heard, yes, yes, there were such occurrences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, before that, during the summer, you were in Borovo Selo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you establish then that on the 4th of July the first mass killings of Serbs were perpetrated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall. No. Which is not to say that this didn't happen. I'm just saying that I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, are you aware of the fact that 20 people were executed by the children's medical centre in Vukovar, and then in Zelica Ulica again over 20 people were executed by a firing squad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in both of these streets, but I did not hear about this, about the execution of children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's being put is there was an execution by the children's medical centre. Which may or may not be true, we don't know. It's just being suggested by the accused. As far as you're concerned, you didn't hear anything about it. Is that right, Mr. Dulovic, if it did occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 20 children --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about children, Mr. Dulovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you talking about the execution of children?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not talking about the execution of children. I was saying that 20 persons were executed near the children's medical centre in Vukovar. I'm not talking about the execution of children at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The children's medical centre is a location --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who were these 20 people who were executed? Of what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb civilians, Mr. Robinson. Serb civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Dulovic, let it be quite clear: I'm talking about all these crimes that were committed during the course of the summer and considerably before the attacks that were aimed at deblockading the military barracks. Are you aware of what happened on the 15th of August when soldiers were attacked, soldiers who did not even have any weapons? They were attacked by the railroad. There is information concerning two Ustashas, as they called themselves, Miljkovic and Zrinjic. This Zrinjic took the gold teeth of this soldier out with a knife and then slit his throat. Do you know about the kind of war that was being waged there in Vukovar and are you aware of the degree of cruelty involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that event. As for the degree of cruelty, I heard a lot about that, and I read about it in the newspapers. For example, that in Borovo Naselje, 40 Serb babies, young children from kindergarten, were slaughtered and put in plastic bags. This is what all the newspapers wrote. I was there, my colleague Gulan from Borba also. We checked this out. Nobody ever gave a shred of evidence that this was true. These were lies in the media. And their only objective was to revolt the Serbs so that they would fight successfully. So these slaughters, all of this, I would have to see that in order to make any such claims. It was absolutely proven that none of these stories that were written about all over and that were talked about over radio and television were mere lies, lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just so I can get a better understanding of your case, are you saying that the attack on Vukovar in the autumn was a defensive response to the summer attacks on the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, matters are actually far more complex than that. During the summer, 1.000 Serbs were killed in Vukovar, and military barracks were blocked. The witness referred to that. And the army launched an action to deblock the military barracks in the centre of Vukovar. Their power had been cut off, all supplies, and they were being shot at from all round. So crimes were committed against the civilian population too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When did the army launch this attack to deblock the military barracks? What month was this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness can say that for himself. This was only in October, as far as I can see. Or perhaps it was even the beginning of November. But the witness can say this himself. Everything that happened during the summer preceded this action, that is to say, the deblockade -- the blockade of the barracks, the killing of civilians, et cetera. Mr. Robinson, I'm going to get to all of that. I have here a written statement that was taken out of a case file. Dragutin Guzovski is the name of the witness involved. He was director of the public utilities company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have a good understanding now of the case that you're putting. So you may proceed with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just finish with this Mr. Robinson. He says here, because he was manager of the public utilities and he had funerals and graveyards under his -- under him as well, Croats were buried at the Catholic cemetery and Serbs were buried at sports stadiums and various streets, et cetera, upon orders given by the authorities in Vukovar. Hundreds and hundreds of them. And he talks about this. This is a handwritten statement of his. This is to say that he was not burying soldiers of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... to that. So let us wait until you get to that piece of evidence and you will try to adduce it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know at all why certain units, when all of this is borne in mind and certain volunteers, why they were in Vukovar itself or in the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In order to take Vukovar and enter it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dulovic, are the reasons clear to you? I mentioned at least some of them, that is to say, these mass killings, mass funerals --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is something we're going to have to determine, as to what the background is to this. It's not for the witness to say. He gives his evidence as to what he saw himself and heard himself. We will have to make a decision as to why all this happened. It's not for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, for example, do you know that on the 20th of August, those who did it testified about it later and they were arrested by the military authorities, a girl, Sladjana Petrovic, in block 1E, she was 25 years old, she was carrying milk, they say: "We stopped her, hit her, and she fell onto the grass. We tied her hands, took off her trousers, then we tied her legs and we had her spread out that way, and I slit her stomach because she said Zrnic was an Ustasha. Zrnic then asked me to cut off her jaw and I cut off her lower jaw and I gave it to Zrnic." Did you hear anything about such events? Did you bear this in mind? Or when he said: "I slaughtered this soldier. I grabbed him by the hair with one hand and then I slit his throat with -- halfway and then Zrnic grabbed me and then he cut his throat completely."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How can the witness possibly answer a series of things? It's not fair on him. Now, you were being asked first of all about an attack on a girl which apparently took place on the 20th of August. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not even the slaughter of this soldier, et cetera, et cetera? I'm just giving some individual examples here, because I realise that you were using various individual examples. So I don't find this very clear that you do not have a single individual example referring to what was quite well known in Vukovar and the surrounding area. So you don't know anything about this, and you've never heard of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. I have no reason not to speak about this if I knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that, for example, even before the military court in Belgrade there was a trial of some persons arrested by the army who had committed crimes? For example, they massacred people while cleansing Vinogradska street. That's a street in Vukovar. You were probably there at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this trial was held in closed session, was closed to the public. I would have gone to such a trial, always.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I guess so, because you spent most of your career as a journalist following trials. Here is the indictment and the judgement is also here. For example, this is against Marko Filkovic, Zdenko Stefancic, Mire Dunatov. It says that they brought in a Serb, Predrag Ciric, into the basement where Filkovic's headquarters were, then they started interrogating him about whether he belonged to the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where is this taking place?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Vukovar. And Stefancic put his pistol into Ciric's mouth and threatened to kill him. And in order to intimidate Ciric and to coerce him to confess, they took him out to the backyard, showed him six males corpses and, afterwards, Stefancic killed Ciric by firing eight bullets from his pistol. Did you hear anything about these crimes that trials were being held about at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you have any details as to where this was happening? I'm not talking about Vukovar, but was this in a factory in Borovo, for example, or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What I have here is the entire indictment. It was happening in Vukovar. And this had to do with the cleansing drive of the Vinogracka Ulica in Vukovar, and I assume you are familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know anything about this. I know that what was being referred to was that a woman was committing crimes in a factory. I don't know whether it was Vuteks or Borovo, the footwear factory. But I don't know anything more about that except that I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to a woman called Ksenija Piplica, also known as Senka, born in 1967?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember her name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: She took part in taking away three unidentified persons in the direction of Dunav, the old slaughterhouse, where these civilians were liquidated and she killed two of them by shooting from a pistol after which the corpses were pushed by her and the guardsman into the Danube.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is a judgement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you wish, Mr. May, I can adduce it into evidence just like the one I have previously quoted. However, I do not have the impression that you are interested in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Prosecution have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Prosecution has an opportunity to view these documents and they are certified copies of the court that rendered the judgement, the Prosecution would not have any objection to the entry of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us have the judgement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give it to you a little later, because I have another question to put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just conclude: You knew nothing about the fact that several months before the events you describe in Vukovar, the liquidation of Serbs in Vukovar was going on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you perhaps hear that Marin Vidic, who was a representative, an emissary of the Croatian authorities for Vukovar, said in his diary of the 4th of September, 1991, on page 111, he said: "The Serbs are in town and we must get rid of all of them"? Did you hear of these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't read about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that among the murderers in Vukovar, there were many well-known criminals, such as Drazen Gazo who, before that, was convicted several times? Did you hear of him and his crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't recall that name. I don't remember this Drazen Gazo you refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how the owner of the Grmec catering establishment in Borovo Naselje was killed, and he was killed by this man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have here court files saying that on an unknown day in October 1991 - and this is about the murder in Grmec - the members of this unit, this paramilitary unit, the Ustashas, threw an explosive into the Grmec catering establishment owned by a man of Serbian nationality, Sucevic, who was an invalid, and they killed him; and in July 1991, on an unknown date, the facilities of the civilian defence, a Serb was brought in, his name was Milenko --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- he was tortured there and his body was thrown into the Danube. And then there was a trial held against Zoran Sipos, also a member of these groups of murderers who were marauding through Vukovar. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this. I'm not saying that such things did not happen, but I know nothing about them. I could not have known. You're talking about Borovo Naselje. The journalists first entered Borovo Naselje on the day Vukovar fell. On that day, I was there, but even had these things happened, I did not have time to find out about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about the events on the 28th of October, this same Zoran Sipos's unit caught some civilians, Zorana Petranovic, Miladen Jovic, Radovana Vukicevic, Jovice Leskovac, also known as Vojo, a man called Dekic, and made them dig trenches in a place where shells were landing, after which they killed them. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Nikola Cibaric, who was also killed by that same group? Do you know anything about this? No, you don't, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I am reading all these examples from court files. So this is not taken from the papers which, as you say, were writing in a sensationalist manner but from records of court proceedings. Did you perhaps hear, because this is really a morbid event, when you were in Vukovar what Nikola Pilipovic, also known as Siptar, did, who committed sexual acts over the dead bodies of Serbian soldiers? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that General Spegelj mentions it in his book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't read it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd object. It seems clear that the witness has said he was only in Vukovar for three months. I would ask Mr. Milosevic to confine any questions just to any of these events. It seems he may be he entitled to question the witness regarding whether he knows of those events within that three-month period, but it seems now we're going into all sorts of matters that we have no connection to time and whether this witness has any possibility of having any relevant knowledge about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well. Please, then, take these court records, if you're interested, and have a look at them, and after that you can decide -- yes, here you are. The complete files are in the possession of my associates, and I can deliver them to you. These are indictments and judgements, and you may be interested in them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The most straightforward course is to exhibit these as one exhibit for identification. At least, we'll exhibit them, give them an exhibit number. They will then be -- they will then be translated. The Prosecution, meanwhile, can have a look at them, and if there's any objection, we'll hear it in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be marked Defence Exhibit 54, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just mention there are some handwritten notes here, but I can get them from my associates without the markings that I made, and they will be handed over as court files. I have underlined some things, marked certain passages, and so on and so forth. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you have not read Spegelj's book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you hear about the crimes perpetrated by Borislav Vukovic from Slatina and Pero Janjic, also known as Tromblon? Did you hear anything about that while you were in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Dulovic. Since you were interested in courts, do you know that this Vukovic admitted to killing soldiers not only while he was ambushing them but also at close range?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have already said, I do not doubt that very probably things like that happened, but I really don't know anything about them. If I knew anything about them, I would say so. This was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Dulovic. Does the name Jastreb mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was Jastreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jastreb was a man called Mile Dedakovic, and he was the commander of the defence of Vukovar. That was what he was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember his order which read verbatim "Anyone who imprisons a Chetnik, let him take him home because I have no use for him"? And everybody interpreted this to mean that prisoners should be killed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not have heard this because this was happening inside Vukovar and I was outside Vukovar, not among the Croats but among the Serbian volunteers and soldiers, those who were holding Vukovar under siege. So how could I have heard this? How could I know what Dedakovic was ordering his men to do in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the name of Zlatko Jankovic, who killed a fighter from World War II, an invalid of the national liberation struggle who had lost both legs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of Marka Filkovica, Knez; Zdenka Stefancic, Plavi? Did you hear about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I noted down the names of people I interviewed, people who told me things, but I know nothing about these names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Dulovic. Do you know anything about the blowing up of Serbian houses? For example, this was done by Ante Budimir. Do you know of this name or do you know anything about the blowing up of Serbian houses in the area of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, for example, in December 1983 [as interpreted] even The New York Times' David Binder wrote of 10.000 Serbian houses that had been blown up with dynamite in Croatia, and he said that Croatia had been totally ethnically cleansed of Serbs, that it was the purest, ethnically purest country in Europe. So how come you know nothing of this and your colleagues who were also there wrote about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe my colleague counted those houses and I did not have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe you heard the statement made by the then Minister of Foreign Affairs, Granic, who said yes, 7.000 Serbian houses have been blown up, not 10.000. So he himself agreed to the number of 7.000 and that no investigations were ever carried out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never listened to Granic speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of Mira and Zvonko Tvorov who themselves killed 30 people from snipers during these actions in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody told me about this, nor do I know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the guardsman, the member of the National Guard Corps Mate Loncar who was especially prominent in these events and who cut off the genitals of his victims and killed in the sight of Dedakovic, that is Jastreb, several civilians? Do you know anything about this? Did anyone tell you about this when you were in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say that Vukovar was shelled without ceasing and that the Croats only fired shots when they were defending themselves from the Serbs. That's what you claim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And throughout all this time you never saw a single event that was taking place in Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have the opportunity to watch what was happening inside Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about commander Ivica Sojic in Vukovar and what he and his group were doing, such as burning corpses, or about what Guzovski was doing since they were questioned by a court and you were a court reporter? So were you ever interested in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never heard anything about this nor were there any indications that these people were on trial or where these trials were being held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have here a handwritten statement by Guzovski. Each page is signed. He says that they did not bury JNA soldiers, that they burned their bodies, the members of the National Guard Corps and the military police of the Republic of Croatia. It says further that Ivan Sojic set up a special group to burn corpses of JNA soldiers, and in the statement here, he says 30, 120, 40 members of these groups or, rather, corpses were buried in stadiums, streets, and so on. Do you know anything about the number of people who were killed and, as you can see, buried by -- there are some sketches of locations of burial sites adduced to this statement; the old cemetery, the mini market, the park, the hospital, the stadium, a mass grave?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you interested, Mr. May, in this statement of the director of the public utilities company in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Go ahead, consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, have you anything to say about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution would object to the admission of this document into evidence. We would certainly welcome Mr. Guzovski, I believe is his name, to appear before the Chamber so the Prosecution could inquire equally into the matters that he has allegedly witnessed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We shan't admit this statement. Hand it back to the accused, please. You can call the witness, of course, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say in your statement on page 3, in the one but last paragraph, that the Serb villages were not damaged, and here you say or, rather, you said yesterday during your oral testimony that the Serb villages were damaged as well but that the Croatian ones were damaged more, as far as I was able to note down. Now, could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And you can see that to this day. If you take the car and go to Vukovar, it depends from one village to the next, but it is quite obvious that the Croatian villages were far more damaged than the Serbian ones, and they follow on from each other, one after another, several of them. Some are smaller, some are bigger, some are more damaged, some are less damaged. So the degree of destruction is not the same in all the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You also explain in the last paragraph on page 3 that you met Veselin Sljivancanin in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said in Negoslavci for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right, yes. And it was clear that he was not responsible to anybody in this combat area. Now, on the basis of what do you say that? How was this clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of his relations with the rest of the officers. That was the opinion I had formed, that he did not answer to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how can you assume that an officer is not responsible to anyone, did not answer to anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I mean in the field of operations. That's what it says quite clearly in that section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, then, you say he pulled out 150 people from a cellar and that he asked -- invited the journalists to go with him to the location, and that they were mostly Croats but that there were also some Serbs among them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What happened was that a situation arose and that foreign journalists were present and so were others as Major Sljivancanin, with a Motorola, called on and allegedly had a conversation with Mile Dedakovic, nicknamed Jastreb, or hook, and we heard him say this. We heard him talking. He said, "Don't allow these people here to die, but you come out and be courageous and share this duel. Let's have a duel."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. That is a sort of epic sequence that related to the fact that actually meant that it was a shame for innocent civilians to die but that if anybody was called upon to die then it should be the two commanders. It was a little archaic and expressed in epic terms but I don't see that it is a crime of any kind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, nobody said that. You asked me what happened, and I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You go on to say that on the 13th of November, you yourself were present when Miroslav Radic with a group of men and with an experienced volunteer prepared to go into action. Are you quite sure that it wasn't the action to save the jeopardised civilians and deblock the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was an attack on a water tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A water tower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the Croats who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the snipers up on the water tower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that civilians live and reside up on a water tower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that Aleksandar Bojkovski, known as Sasa, called you to show you the corpses of six persons who were members of the ZNG, the Croatian National Guard Corps, and you ascertained that they had been dead for two or three days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would have thought so. I can't actually say what they looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, never mind about the details, but there was something suspicious there. You were suspicious because you didn't see any weapons standing round about. Do you always think that there should be weapons round about people who had been killed in battle fighting the National Guard Corps, Croatian National Guard Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never said that I was -- that this was a suspicious factor. I just noted what I had seen. I said what I had actually seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you say that they were dead for a few days but that there were no weapons beside them, so I assume that you were indicating this and that you thought that there should have been some weapons found round about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I just meant what I said, that there were no weapons to be seen standing round about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these ZNG guard members who were dead for three -- had been dead for three days had no weapons standing round about them. You also go on to say that they were not in uniform or, rather, as I understood you to say yesterday, one of them was wearing a uniform. Others were -- the others were not, or parts of uniforms. Do you know how many participants took place in these operations around Vukovar and people without uniform taking part in them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. There's no way I could know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, then, please, you say you heard the conversation between Vojislav Seselj and a group of officers going on and that you heard him say that it was a great test for the Serbs and that he said that no Ustasha must be allowed to leave Vukovar alive, and you ascribe those words to Seselj. Are you quite certain that you heard him say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
