utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so. Otherwise, I wouldn't have made a note of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say, then, Mr. Dulovic, that in your notebook you recorded only the facts or did you make sketches for the articles you wished to publish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had several notebooks. And this was important for me. It was important for me to hear what the vojvoda was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Dulovic. Is it quite clear that you were endeavouring in this testimony, too, to explain in every possible way, as has been the policy of your entire editorial office, that is to say the Vreme magazine, to put the blame on the Serbs for what had happened there and to all my questions about the crimes that came to pass before, the mass killings, the mass graves, the liquidations and executions of people, blockades of the barracks, your answer to all of that is that you know nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me at what distance you listened in to the conversation that Seselj had.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not listening in. The door was half open, the door was ajar. I wasn't eavesdropping.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me, then, what capacity was Seselj in there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You must ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, at the time, he was an MP in the Assembly, a deputy there and a representative of his own party; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many people attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five or six, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the names of those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them I've already stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You told us all the names you knew of; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that in Borovo you saw many people shut up in the Borovo shoe factory, that they were Croatian civilians, including women and children, that you saw a large quantity of weapons which had quite obviously been handed over. Now, do you make a connection between the large number of persons and the weapons that you saw on the spot, saw there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do link up the two because I was there when they left and when they were boarded onto buses. There were soldiers there and civilians there too, women as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Explain this to me: What happened to those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They got onto the buses and they left or, rather, they were taken away. Now, where they were driven to, we didn't know at that time. We were later told that they had been taken off to Sremska Mitrovica to the prison there, but not only to Sremska Mitrovica - and this is the freshest information that I have, the most recent - but that they were also taken off to a kind of camp near Zrenjanin, to a settlement there or whatever. It was called Begejci and a place called Stajicevo. So the civilians were separated from the soldiers. And this is something that is going to be published and investigated and proved that that was so, that two camps existed in the vicinity of Zrenjanin, the town of Zrenjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for the soldiers that were taken into custody, I assume they were treated like prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as for the women and children, do you assume that anybody arrested women and children or was this some sort of operation that the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. army engaged in to care for the women and children, not to leave them in the war stricken area, to put them up somewhere? Did anything happen to those people, the people who were put up in a collection centre? There were no camps in Serbia, nor do I know that the army had any camps at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know under whose competence they came, they were placed, but what I'm saying is quite correct. These people were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say they were handed over to the Red Cross and then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is that they were exchanged with the Serbs that had been held captive. Some sort of bargain was struck along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you have any knowledge or information that these people who were either taken prisoner as soldiers or put up in collection centres as civilians, that anything happened to any of those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Nobody is saying that. Nobody is claiming that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you say that you noticed that the situation was one of anarchy, that everybody did some shooting during the night, shooted about as they saw fit. You say you spoke to two volunteers who were drunk. What part of town were you visiting at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the part of town that is referred to as Sajmiste. It is a part of town which is populated exclusively by Serbs. At least, that street was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you also say that a man, on the 21st of November, told you that they went around killing in Ovcara from 5.00 in the afternoon until 1.00 in the morning. And I don't want to repeat all the other things that you stated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like us to take a look at your statement together. You referred to your statement yesterday, so let's take a look at it together. Let me just find the portion that I'm looking for. I assume that you were called in as a witness and that the events were the subject of an investigation. Isn't that so, Mr. Dulovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say the following: That the criminal proceedings were taken against perpetrators unknown, perpetrator unknown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's in the plural, I made a mistake saying it in the singular. In the plural, against perpetrators unknown, persons unknown, and on the basis of that, you note that the court or, rather, the prosecution did not have the intention of identifying the actual perpetrators. Have I understood you properly, what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You understood very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Now, you go on to say that -- and I understood you to say yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry to interrupt, Mr. Milosevic. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that as an experienced journalist in court affairs, because your job was to follow court trials, that you knew that a case is raised against unidentified perpetrators when the perpetrators cannot be identified. And you say on page 4 of your testimony or report here: "Later on, for many years on the basis of this description -- several years later, based on this description, I accidentally learnt that this could have been a certain Slavisa Pavlovic from Smederevo. I do not know where this man is now or whether he is alive, nor did I check if this information was correct." So in this statement of yours, you do not -- the one you give as a witness, you say you do not know whether the facts are correct. You indicate the possibility of this having been a man called Slavisa Pavlovic from Smederevo who was responsible, and the proceedings, the lawsuit was raised against perpetrators unknown. And you are taking part as a witness, and in your testimony you indicate the possibility, just the possibility that it might be a man called Slavisa Pavlovic. So before you indicated the possibility of it having been this man, did you have in mind a certain name, or if you pointed out this possibility, for you -- and you yourself say that you didn't check the information out, that they were able, and I'm asking you this as an experienced journalist who attended the work of courts, that this indictment should be rephrased with the name of Slavisa Pavlovic contained in it before further investigations were undertaken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ask me a question now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is this: As far as I remember, you said that the state was not interested in uncovering this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not mention the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. The authorities. The court. It doesn't matter now. That they weren't interested in uncovering, unravelling this whole affair, which means that the authorities bring this case to court, and I'm talking about the court authorities, how then are you able to conclude that the authorities weren't interested in ascertaining who was responsible for committing this act?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I think that at that particular point in time, the authorities were not interested in really and truly bringing perpetrators to justice but that this was all a farce. All of this was a farce. And this man, Slavisa Pavlovic, whom I talk about here, when he talked to me or, rather, not me but there were several of us, when he told us what the shooting in Ovcara looked like, I described this. However, his name -- I heard his name from a man who ought to have known about it, and he was in charge of controlling and going after criminals. So I didn't see him in Vukovar, but he was there, and this is something that I heard from a general, General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, who after a certain amount of time, later on when I recounted the event to him, after that he told me that the man in question was a man named Slavisa Pavlovic from Smederevo, and I assume that that was something that the army had to have known or, rather, the court, if it seriously wanted to persecute and bring to justice, bring to trial war criminals. But there was no serious intent in that direction on the part of the authorities, as you call them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to have to interrupt now because it's time to adjourn. Mr. Milosevic, we can continue in the morning. You will have two hours left for cross-examination of this witness on the time that we have allowed. We will adjourn now. Would you be back, please, Mr. Dulovic, at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 18th day of October, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: [Closed session made public by later order of the chamber]
[Trial Chamber and senior legal officer confer]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
